title: Query-Conditioned Marginals for OT-Based Context Compression: An Empirical Investigation

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to make optimal-transport (OT) context compression query-aware, ensuring that capacity is not wasted on task-irrelevant tokens. This specific objective — introducing query-awareness into OT-based context compression — is not directly addressed in any prior paper. While several papers discuss context compression (e.g., [1], [2], [4], [6]), none explicitly aim to optimize OT-based compression by incorporating query relevance into the sender marginals. For example, [6] introduces KVzip, which is query-agnostic, and [4] focuses on extractive compression but does not modify OT marginals based on query relevance. Therefore, no prior paper shares this purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, QCap-OT, modifies the OT sender marginals in Sinkhorn-based ComprExIT using query-anchor similarity, requiring no retraining or additional parameters. This mechanism is a novel adaptation of the Sinkhorn algorithm. While several papers use Sinkhorn-based OT (e.g., [9], [10], [12], [13], [17], [25]), none implement a query-aware reweighting of sender marginals. For instance, [9] introduces importance sparsification for Sinkhorn but does not involve query relevance, and [17] applies OT to partial domain adaptation without query-specific adjustments. Thus, no prior paper implements a substantively equivalent mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves comparing QCap-OT to vanilla ComprExIT, showing statistical indistinguishability (F1 delta approximately 0, p > 0.05). This evaluation design — comparing a modified OT-based method to its vanilla counterpart using statistical tests — is covered by prior work. For example, [9] evaluates Spar-Sink by comparing it to standard Sinkhorn, and [17] evaluates MOT by comparing it to baseline OT methods. The specific benchmark or dataset differs, but the evaluation design (comparison to a baseline OT method with statistical validation) is equivalent.

### Domain
The domain is LLM context compression. This domain is covered by prior papers such as [1], [2], [4], and [6], which all address context compression for LLMs. While the specific sub-problem (query-aware OT-based compression) is new, the general application area of LLM context compression is not.

Paper [3] (SharedLLM) explicitly mentions "query-aware information retrieval" in the context of context compression for LLMs. Paper [4] (AdaComp) focuses on retaining "query-relevant sentences" in context compression. Paper [7] (Quest) pursues query-aware sparsity for efficient long-context LLM inference — the objective is making token selection/compression query-aware to avoid wasting capacity on irrelevant tokens. These all share the same problem-class objective: make context compression/token selection query-aware to avoid wasting capacity on irrelevant content. Paper [7] is the closest match: "query-aware sparsity" for LLM inference where "a small portion of critical tokens will dominate the attention outcomes."

**MECHANISM: Reweighting OT sender marginals in Sinkhorn-based compression according to query-anchor similarity, inference-only, no retraining.**

The mechanism has two components: (1) Sinkhorn/OT-based compression with marginal reweighting, and (2) query-similarity-based reweighting at inference time without retraining. Paper [19] (MOTOR) uses optimal transport for retrieval reranking based on query relevance in a multimodal setting. Paper [17] (MOT) uses masked OT where transport plan weights are modified based on relevance signals. Paper [8] uses attention-guided OT where attention scores reweight the OT problem. None of these specifically reweight Sinkhorn *sender marginals* based on query-anchor similarity for LLM context compression. The specific primitive of modifying marginal distributions in Sinkhorn to inject query relevance is not clearly present. Paper [8] is closest ("Attention-Guided Optimal Transport" where attention reweights OT), but it's in domain adaptation, not context compression. The underlying primitive — reweighting OT marginals by a relevance/attention signal — does appear in [8] and [17]. Paper [8] uses attention scores to guide OT, which is substantively equivalent to using query-anchor similarity to reweight OT marginals.

**EVALUATION: Statistical indistinguishability from baseline (F1 delta ≈ 0, p > 0.05) across metrics.**

The evaluation design here is a null-result statistical significance test comparing a proposed method to a baseline using standard NLP metrics (F1) with p-value reporting. This is a standard statistical comparison framework used broadly. However, the specific claim being validated — that the method is *statistically indistinguishable* from a baseline — is an unusual evaluation design where the goal is to show no significant difference. Looking through the papers, none explicitly use this "equivalence testing" or "null result" statistical framework as their primary evaluation design. Standard significance testing appears in many papers, but the specific design of demonstrating statistical equivalence (p > 0.05 as a positive result) is not clearly present in any prior paper listed.

**DOMAIN: LLM context compression.**

Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6] all work in LLM context compression. This is clearly covered.
